hero.headline: Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez resigns after Senate confirms him as ambassador to Brazil
hero.teaser: Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez has resigned from the Florida House of Representatives after the U.S. Senate confirmed his nomination as Ambassador to the Federative Republic of
hero.body:
Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez has resigned from the Florida House of Representatives after the U.S. Senate confirmed his nomination as Ambassador to the Federative Republic of Brazil. Perez announced his resignation in a letter to House members, saying President Donald J. Trump asked him to serve in the ambassadorial role. His resignation from the Florida House takes effect Friday, Aug. 21, and he will take the oath of office as ambassador later this month.

 Under House Rule 2.5(d), Speaker pro tempore Wyman Duggan will assume the duties, powers, and prerogatives of the Speaker. Perez stated in his resignation letter that he has notified Speaker-designate Sam Garrison that his team may take control of House operations on Sept. 8 to allow more time to prepare for the start of his term. The transition creates a brief window where Duggan will serve as acting speaker before Garrison assumes the role.

 In his resignation letter, Perez reflected on his tenure leading the chamber. He described serving in the House and as Speaker as the honor of his life. Perez told members they have been on a sometimes thrilling and sometimes tumultuous journey together during his time in leadership.

 Perez expressed hope that House members feel, as he does, that they have done right by the House and the people of Florida as they look back on this term. The resignation marks the end of his service in the Florida Legislature as he prepares to represent the United States in Brazil. Perez becomes the latest Florida state legislator to leave office for a federal appointment under the Trump administration.

cards.headline: Florida property tax amendment draws organized opposition while supporters remain quiet
cards.teaser: A proposed constitutional amendment to cut property taxes in Florida is facing mounting organized opposition while support remains largely silent. Groups representing police, firef
cards.body:
A proposed constitutional amendment to cut property taxes in Florida is facing mounting organized opposition while support remains largely silent. Groups representing police, firefighters, sheriffs, hospitals, cities and counties have raised alarms about Amendment 3, warning the proposed tax cut could hollow out local budgets and jeopardize police, fire, emergency medical and other services.

 The Republican-controlled Legislature placed Amendment 3 on the November ballot during a June special session. Under the proposal, the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes would increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The amendment would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. A state fiscal analysis estimates the amendments quantifiable provisions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion during the 2027-28 fiscal year, eventually reaching approximately $11.83 billion annually.

 Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd called the proposal a train wreck during a Tuesday news conference. The Florida Sheriffs Association said it is significantly concerned about the proposal. The Florida State Fraternal Order of Police has formally opposed it, while the Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association warned that it could undermine public-safety funding without providing a replacement revenue source. On Wednesday, the No On Three campaign announced endorsements from 31 Democratic state lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell and Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman.

 Governor Ron DeSantis called the special session that produced the proposal and said he will vote for it, but made clear the Legislature's final product fell short of what he wanted. Attorney General James Uthmeier paired support for tax relief with concern about potential consequences. U.S. Senator Rick Scott initially appeared skeptical but later announced he would vote for Amendment 3. No comparable statewide Yes On Three campaign has publicly materialized.

 A July University of North Florida poll found 61% support when likely voters were told the amendment would begin phasing out non-school homestead taxes, only one percentage point above the 60% constitutional threshold needed to pass. Support fell to 45% when respondents were also told that estimates suggested the proposal could create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over its first two years. Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled this week that the title and summary written by lawmakers were biased, misleading and factually inaccurate, ordering Attorney General Uthmeier to submit a replacement within 10 days.

cards.headline: Tom Rahill wins $10,000 grand prize in 2026 Florida Python Challenge after removing 96 snakes
cards.teaser: The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and its partners announced the results of the 2026 Florida Python Challenge on Wednesday. Tom Rahill won the Ultimate Grand Pr
cards.body:
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and its partners announced the results of the 2026 Florida Python Challenge on Wednesday. Tom Rahill won the Ultimate Grand Prize of $10,000 after removing 96 Burmese pythons from Everglades National Park during the 10-day competition. A total of 907 participants from 30 states, Canada and Vietnam collectively removed 280 invasive Burmese pythons from South Florida.

 Rahm Levinson removed the longest python of the competition, a 16-foot, 5-inch snake, also from Everglades National Park. A highlight of this year's event was the return of Everglades National Park as a partner and one of eight official competition locations. The event was hosted by the FWC and the South Florida Water Management District, in partnership with the National Park Service and the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida.

 In the professional category, Christina Kraus won $2,500 for most pythons with 36 snakes removed, and Taylor Stanberry won $1,500 as runner-up with 34 pythons. Rahm Levinson also won $1,000 for the longest python prize. In the novice category, Bart Shreve won $2,500 for removing nine pythons, Michael Marousky won $1,500 for four pythons, and Vincent Poole won $1,000 for an 8-foot, 2-inch snake. In the military category for active duty and veterans, Stephen Payton of the U.S. Army won $2,500 for three pythons, Jonathan Miller of the U.S. Air Force won $1,500 for two pythons, and Jeffery 'Heath' Roser of the U.S. Army won $1,000 for an 8-foot, 7-inch python.

 FWC Chairman Rodney Barreto said the number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades is a major victory for Florida's native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation. South Florida Water Management District Governing Board Member 'Alligator Ron' Bergeron said removing Burmese pythons from the ecosystem is critical to the survival of native species that call the area home. The 10-day event is designed to raise awareness about invasive species and engage the public in Everglades conservation through the removal of invasive Burmese pythons.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General threatens Catholic school scholarship funding over vaccine exemption policies
cards.teaser: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state la
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state law or risk losing access to state scholarship funding. In a letter to Catholic school leaders, Uthmeier argues state law requires schools to accept religious vaccine exemptions even if church leaders disagree. He also cites Vatican teaching on individual conscience in making his case.

 The financial stakes are significant. More than 525,000 Florida students use state scholarship programs, including roughly 92 percent of Catholic school students. Uthmeier has warned that schools could lose access to those programs if they do not comply. Existing policies at some Catholic schools, including one in Orlando, state that vaccines are not against Catholic teaching and that allowing exemptions could endanger students and staff.

 The clash follows Governor Ron DeSantis' broader campaign against vaccine mandates. Lawmakers rejected proposals this year to eliminate Florida's remaining school vaccine requirements or create a broader conscience exemption. Medical and religious opt-outs remain available.

 The Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops has not yet answered the argument directly. Michele Taylor of the Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops said the organization is reviewing the letter and will respond to the Attorney General by his requested date of August 7.

 State Democrats are calling the attorney general's demands a distraction. Rep. Daryl Campbell, a Fort Lauderdale Democrat, pointed to what he called more pressing concerns facing Floridians.

 Campbell said affordability has been the crisis of this generation. The bishops have until Friday to respond to Uthmeier's letter. For now, his scholarship threat remains a warning, not a funding cutoff.

cards.headline: Florida judge orders rewrite of Amendment 3 ballot language, calling it biased and misleading
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge has ordered Florida to rewrite the ballot language for Amendment 3, a sweeping property-tax proposal, ruling that the Legislature's description is biased, inacc
cards.body:
A Leon County judge has ordered Florida to rewrite the ballot language for Amendment 3, a sweeping property-tax proposal, ruling that the Legislature's description is biased, inaccurate and misleading. Circuit Judge David Frank granted summary judgment to challengers Monday night, declared the current title and summary clearly and conclusively defective, and blocked Secretary of State Cord Byrd from placing that wording on the November ballot.

 Frank ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to submit corrected language to the Department of State within 10 days. The decision does not remove Amendment 3 itself from the ballot. The judge stressed that the court is not deciding whether the property-tax plan is good policy, only whether voters are receiving a fair and accurate explanation before making that decision.

 Three consolidated lawsuits challenged the title Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes and a summary promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness. Frank agreed that the title resembles campaign messaging more than a neutral description. The title is more akin to a political slogan, Frank wrote.

 It is not fair or neutral. It advocates a policy position: to stop excessive property taxes. The judge found the word save was designed to provoke an emotional response.

 He also ruled that invoking Save Our Homes could confuse voters because that name is already commonly associated with Florida's existing 3 percent cap on annual assessment increases for homesteaded property. Amendment 3 would not change that cap.

 Frank directed Uthmeier to remove the summary's opening declaration that the amendment benefits Florida taxpayers and four promotional taglines: Exempting homestead properties from taxation, Ensuring funding for core services, Protecting small businesses and Ensuring fairness for Florida residents. The judge found several additional problems with the description.

 The summary says the amendment would exempt the first $250,000 of a homestead's value when it takes effect in 2027. The proposal would actually set the exemption at $150,000 during 2027 before increasing it to $250,000 in 2028 and adjusting it for inflation beginning in 2029. The court also rejected language promising a schedule for full elimination of non-school homestead property taxes. The amendment would instead require lawmakers to establish a procedure through which cities and counties could increase the exemption up to a home's full assessed value.

 The Legislature approved Amendment 3 during a June special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis. For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.

 School district property taxes would remain unaffected. The measure would also reduce the assessment-growth cap for non-homestead property from 10 percent to 5 percent. Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year.

 The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Amendment 3 requires support from at least 60 percent of voters to pass in November.

cards.headline: Florida Sheriffs Association warns homestead exemption ballot measure could lengthen law enforcement response times
cards.teaser: The statewide association says a November ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners could create longer law enforcement response times.
cards.body:
The Florida Sheriffs Association has entered the tax reform debate, raising concerns about a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners. The association states it has significant concerns with the referendum, warning it could potentially create longer law enforcement response times. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said the association's position carries weight, noting that Florida sheriffs are always moderate in their responses and tend to be very supportive of the governor, making their opposition to the governor in this case a clear signal.

 Snyder said he understands the frustration driving the push for tax relief but warned the savings may come with hidden costs. He explained that instead of paying for services out of their left pocket, taxpayers will pay for it out of their right pocket, as sheriffs' offices and fire departments would look to other taxes and fees to make up the difference. Snyder served as Martin County sheriff for 12 years and managed the department's budgets throughout that time.

 Snyder said his department looked at every single nickel and could shave a little off the edges, but when 80 percent of the budget is personnel services, unless deputies or firefighters are let go, there is not much that can be done with the budget. The debate over cutting taxes and its impact on public safety is central to the amendment question facing voters in November. County and city leaders are grappling with how they would manage significant cuts in revenue as homeowners look to Tallahassee for relief from high tax bills.

cards.headline: Honduran national convicted in Fort Pierce federal court for firearms trafficking to Honduras
cards.teaser: A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them
cards.body:
A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them to Honduras. Luis Matute Figueroa, 33, of Lake Worth, was found guilty of conspiracy and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Monday.

 Matute Figueroa overstayed a tourist visa in 2017 and remained in the United States without lawful status. WhatsApp messages recovered during the investigation showed that Matute Figueroa provided co-conspirators with firearm inventories, pricing information and shipping instructions for weapons destined for Honduras. The messages also contained a photograph and a video of Matute Figueroa in possession of a distinctive gold Colt 1911 pistol. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe said the defendant exploited his unlawful presence in the United States to help traffic American firearms to Honduras.

 Court records and trial evidence showed that Matute Figueroa conspired with Gerson Eliu Padilla-Figueroa, Juan Matute Figueroa, Ariel Henriquez-Padilla, and William Mendoza to acquire firearms in the United States through straw purchases and illegally export them to Honduras. Straw purchases involve using individuals with clean records to buy firearms on behalf of those prohibited from owning them.

 Matute Figueroa faces up to five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count and up to 15 years in prison on the firearm possession count. A federal district court judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The ATF Miami Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations Miami investigated the case with assistance from the Broward Sheriff's Office, the Martin County Sheriff's Office, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Attorney Suzanne Huyler is prosecuting the case.

hero.headline: Martin County schools open Monday with new school bus safety measures and earlier start times
hero.teaser: The 2026-2027 school year begins Monday, Aug. 10 for all students in Martin County, with 12 elementary schools opening at 7:40 a.m., four high schools including Indiantown High Sch
hero.body:
The 2026-2027 school year begins Monday, Aug. 10 for all students in Martin County, with 12 elementary schools opening at 7:40 a.m., four high schools including Indiantown High School charter school starting at 8:30 a.m., and five middle schools beginning at 9:20 a.m. The earlier elementary school start times mean many students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter, particularly Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District bus transportation schedules.

 The Martin County School District is urging parents, students and motorists to observe school bus safety rules throughout the 2026-27 school year. Students should arrive at their bus stop 5 to 10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver's instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street, said Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations. She encouraged families to review their child's bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop.

 Florida law requires drivers to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to six months.

 The Martin County School District's transportation page at www.martinschools.org/page/transportation provides information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. Parents are encouraged to supervise younger children while they wait for the bus, remind children to wait for the driver's signal before crossing the street, and ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors.

cards.headline: Martin County firefighters rescue tree trimmer trapped 40 feet in air in Stuart
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue crews on Saturday afternoon freed a tree trimmer who became trapped about 40 feet in the air after his lift stopped working in Stuart. Firefighters were d
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue crews on Saturday afternoon freed a tree trimmer who became trapped about 40 feet in the air after his lift stopped working in Stuart. Firefighters were dispatched around 1 p.m. to find the man stuck on the lift, which had stopped moving up and down while he was trimming trees in the area.

 Limited access for a ladder forced crews to use a specialized high-angle rescue approach. Firefighters first removed nearby tree limbs, then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to the ground.

 Paramedics evaluated the man once he reached the ground and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital.

 Martin County Fire Rescue credited C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for completing the rescue.

cards.headline: Costco in Stuart reopens after electrical fire with limited inventory
cards.teaser: The Costco at 3173 Kanner Highway in Stuart has reopened following an electrical fire that temporarily closed the store on Thursday. Store management told the Stuart Police Departm
cards.body:
The Costco at 3173 Kanner Highway in Stuart has reopened following an electrical fire that temporarily closed the store on Thursday. Store management told the Stuart Police Department that only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit is not operational.

 The Stuart Police Department said the electrical fire at the Kanner Highway location has been extinguished. Shoppers and travelers were asked to avoid the area while the store was closed.

 The fire disrupted normal operations at the Martin County location. The store has since resumed limited service while the refrigeration system remains down.

 Customers visiting the Stuart Costco can purchase dry goods but will not be able to buy refrigerated or frozen items until the refrigeration unit is repaired.

cards.headline: Costco in Stuart reopens after electrical fire but refrigeration remains down
cards.teaser: The Costco at 3173 S. Kanner Highway in Stuart reopened Friday after an electrical fire forced its closure Thursday, but only dry goods are available because the refrigeration unit remains non-operational.
cards.body:
A Costco in Stuart reopened Friday with limited services after an electrical fire forced the store to close Thursday afternoon. The store at 3173 S. Kanner Highway is now open but only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit remains non-operational, according to the Stuart Police Department.

 The electrical fire was reported at around 4 p.m. Thursday. The Stuart Police Department said out of an abundance of caution the store was closed following the fire, which was extinguished by Stuart and Martin County Fire Rescue personnel. Authorities urged individuals to avoid the area while the store remained closed Thursday.

 Store management confirmed to the Stuart Police Department that customers cannot purchase refrigerated or frozen items until the refrigeration system is restored. The police department shared the update about the limited inventory available at the location.

 The Costco location serves Stuart and surrounding Martin County communities. The store had been closed for an undetermined amount of time Thursday while fire rescue personnel remained on scene to ensure the building was safe to reopen.

cards.headline: Piper's Landing residents plant 6,000 mangroves to restore eroded St. Lucie River island in Martin County
cards.teaser: Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club in Martin County are planting 6,000 mangroves to restore a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroye
cards.body:
Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club in Martin County are planting 6,000 mangroves to restore a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed. The community spent two years cultivating the red and white mangroves in an on-site nursery before beginning the planting work in the St. Lucie River waterway.

 Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, rallied her neighbors to take action after watching the mangroves deteriorate. The community built 10 planter pools to grow the mangroves, collecting red and white seeds from their mangrove island. Residents were at the nursery almost every day to inspect the plants, water them when needed, monitor their health, and match salinity to the river conditions.

 The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. With the nursery phase complete, residents brought in Keith Rossin, CEO of Mang Consulting Services, to do the planting. Rossin said the project uses dredge fill brought up to the right elevation for the mangroves, creating mangrove habitat in a way he has never seen done before.

 The thousands of small trees are expected to grow into the foundation of a new ecosystem. Standing said residents will be able to go down to the mangrove island and enjoy a beautiful lush island once the restoration is complete.

hero.headline: F-bombs fly in confrontation over Port St. Lucie campaign signs
hero.teaser: A profanity-laced confrontation was captured on video between mayoral challenger Steve Giordano and the husband of incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin.
hero.body:
As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. The incidents prompted the Port St. Lucie Police Department to launch investigations into two separate cases involving campaign signs, one of which led to a confrontation.

 During the overnight hours Friday, Aug. 7, Giordano told CBS12 News that he and his campaign manager were putting up signs near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter.

 The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin, with the two shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission.

 Police said investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools reopen Monday with new bus safety warnings
cards.teaser: Public school for all students in St. Lucie County begins Monday, Aug. 10, with the St. Lucie County School District and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office urging parents, students,
cards.body:
Public school for all students in St. Lucie County begins Monday, Aug. 10, with the St. Lucie County School District and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office urging parents, students, and motorists to exercise caution around school buses throughout the 2026-27 school year. The seven high schools will open for students as early as 7:33 a.m., and the daily start of school for eleven K-8 grade schools is 7:35 a.m.

 Lincoln Park Academy in Fort Pierce begins its days at 7:23 a.m. Dan McCarty and Forest Grove middle schools start sessions at 9:30 a.m., while the start of school for Southern Oaks and Southport middle schools is at 9:40 a.m.

 Sheriff Richard Del Toro said motorists must obey school zone speed limits and always stop when a school bus displays its flashing red lights and extended stop arm. Parents should review bus stop safety with their children, and students should remain attentive, follow the bus driver's instructions, and never cross the street until they are signaled to do so safely. Lydia Martin, chief communications officer for St. Lucie County School District, said families should allow extra travel time during the first few weeks of school as traffic patterns increase and students adjust to their routines.

 Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to 6 months.

 School district officials recommend parents have children arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early, supervise younger children while they wait, and ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. Students should stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting, never play or run near traffic, and stay out of the bus's danger zone.

 The Here Comes The Bus app can be downloaded at www.herecomesthebus.com. Anyone who sees unsafe driving around school buses, dangerous conditions at bus stops, or suspicious activity near bus stops can report it to local law enforcement or the St. Lucie Public Schools Transportation Department at 772-204-RIDE.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office warns against using social media to report crimes
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office reminded residents to call 911 for crimes in progress after an animal cruelty case was reported through social media tags.
cards.body:
Following the arrest of Ricky Lee Schieferstein on animal cruelty charges after a social media video showed alleged dog abuse, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office issued a reminder about how to report crimes. The sheriff's office said that while it appreciates the public's assistance in bringing incidents to its attention, social media platforms are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

 The fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911, according to the sheriff's office. The case began after numerous members of the community shared a video and tagged the sheriff's office across its social media platforms before the information was turned over to the criminal investigations division.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing developers short $15 million, city commissioners divided on next steps
cards.teaser: The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce faces another delay as Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short
cards.body:
The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce faces another delay as Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project. Live Oak Development CEO Paul Bertozzi said the shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant, but Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied.

 Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun. Commissioners are debating whether the city should reclaim the property.

 Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming. He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for.

 Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait. Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing, including a beer garden and a deli, but the delays are wearing on him.

 The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police investigate two separate campaign sign incidents involving Mayor Martin's husband
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Department released an update Friday on two separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard. The first incident occurred August 5 near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue, where a Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.

 Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.

 The second incident occurred August 7 near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs. During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.

 Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence. The confrontation occurred after Giordano says he saw a man take a sign out of the ground and throw it, according to CBS12 News. The man in the video appears to be Aaron Martin, Shannon Martin's husband and a lieutenant in Port St. Lucie's Police Department.

 Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.

 Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced. The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.

 The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. The department said the fact that Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process, and the investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy. The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures.

 Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation. Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement that her campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of her campaign signs at different locations over several days, and that her husband simply restored the signs that had been removed.

cards.headline: Man charged with burglary, loitering near St. Lucie Village
cards.teaser: A 42-year-old man linked to several burglaries in the St. Lucie Village community was arrested by St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office deputies.
cards.body:
Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, was arrested on August 5 after officers found him going through trash near the road at the 2900 block of North Indian River Drive, according to a St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office Facebook posting. During their investigation, deputies determined Holmes matched the description of a person of interest developed during an ongoing burglary investigation in St. Lucie Village. Through additional investigative efforts, deputies established probable cause linking Holmes to other reported crimes in the area.

 Holmes was charged with two counts of burglary of a conveyance and one count of loitering and prowling. He also had a bicycle with fishing equipment attached. Holmes was taken to the St. Lucie County Jail, where he remained as of August 6 on a $31,000 bond. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the case highlights the value of proactive patrol and the attention to detail deputies demonstrate every day.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools open Monday with some bus pickups before sunrise
hero.teaser: Public schools in Indian River County open Monday, Aug. 10, for the 2026-2027 school year, with high schools starting at 7:20 a.m., middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elem
hero.body:
Public schools in Indian River County open Monday, Aug. 10, for the 2026-2027 school year, with high schools starting at 7:20 a.m., middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elementary schools at 9 a.m. Some students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter, particularly students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district's strategic communications and marketing.

 The School District and Indian River County Sheriff's Office urge all parents, students, and motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety. Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page that all schools are changing and there will be new challenges with drop-offs, pickups, and buses. He asked parents to be patient during drop-off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors.

 At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. The same rule applies to two-lane paved roads. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to six months.

 Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop-off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas, Schafte said. Families should remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street. Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation, as well as the district's Facebook and Instagram accounts.

cards.headline: Indian River County approves expansion of Westside Racquet Club in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Commission approved a special exception use and Phase 1 site plan on August 4 for the renovation and expansion of the Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era fac
cards.body:
The Indian River County Commission approved a special exception use and Phase 1 site plan on August 4 for the renovation and expansion of the Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era facility in Vero Beach that has fallen into disrepair in recent years. The 6.89-acre property is located east of 43rd Avenue Southwest, north of 6th Lane Southwest and south of Fifth Place Southwest.

 Phase 1 of the project will restore the existing eight tennis courts, construct four new padel courts and construct associated site improvements including utilities, stormwater, parking and landscaping. The existing 2,400-square-foot clubhouse will be restored in Phase 2, which will also add two padel courts. Phase 3 will include a pool house and four pickleball courts, while Phase 4 will add two additional tennis courts. The Planning Zoning Commission voted unanimously to recommend approval on June 11 but added a special condition due to concerns about potential noise pollution and light infiltration onto adjacent properties.

 Vice-Chairwoman Laura Moss expressed concerns about voting on the special exception use that would cover all four phases while only approving the Phase 1 site plan, saying commissioners were being asked to vote in the blind. She also raised concerns about pickleball noise and lighting impacts on neighboring residents. Planning Development Services Director John Stoll said the county can require traffic studies once the project exceeds 400 average daily trips and can implement noise mitigation measures including limiting nighttime lighting and operational hours, requiring special paddles and balls, and increasing separation from neighbors.

 District 3 Commissioner Joseph Earman pointed out the continuity of use on the parcel and said he had heard from residents who think the improvements will add value to their property. Mark Jaffe, a 4th Lane Southwest resident, was the only public speaker and said he would like to see the project move forward. The County Commission voted unanimously to approve the requests.

cards.headline: Vero Beach moves forward on $4.7 million Humiston Beach boardwalk reconstruction four years after Hurricane Nicole
cards.teaser: Vero Beach has established a five-person committee to help rebuild the boardwalk at Humiston Beach, which Hurricane Nicole destroyed four years ago. The city currently has $3.1 mil
cards.body:
Vero Beach has established a five-person committee to help rebuild the boardwalk at Humiston Beach, which Hurricane Nicole destroyed four years ago. The city currently has $3.1 million raised toward the $4.7 million project cost, leaving a $1.6 million funding gap that the new committee will work to close through donor outreach and fundraising.

 Vero Beach Councilmember John Carroll said beach use has dropped significantly since the boardwalk's destruction. The committee will develop a fundraising plan and ensure appropriate recognition for donors who have already contributed to the project. The city plans to accept project bids next week.

 Residents including Calista Littleton said they have been waiting to restore normal beach access at the site. Doris DeAngelis said her aunt, who uses a walker, now has only a small area to enjoy the beach due to limited access without the boardwalk.

 If the timeline holds, the city hopes to begin construction in November and complete a new boardwalk by April. DeAngelis said her aunt Mina, who will turn 105 and a half years old, would love to see the boardwalk return.

cards.headline: Early voting begins Saturday across Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River counties for August primary
cards.teaser: Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday across the Treasure Coast, with locations opening in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.
cards.body:
Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday, August 9, and runs through Sunday, August 17, across the Treasure Coast region and surrounding counties. Voters in multiple counties will have the opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the primary election day.

 In Indian River County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find a complete list of early voting locations and additional information at voteindianriver.com.

 In Martin County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find locations and additional information at martinvotes.gov. In St. Lucie County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find locations and additional information at stlucievotes.gov.

 Early voting is also available in Palm Beach County and Okeechobee County during the same period, running Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Palm Beach County voters can visit votepalmbeach.gov for a full list of early voting locations. Okeechobee County voters can find more information at voteokeechobee.gov, though hours were not immediately available at the time of publication.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art hosts free Second Saturday events Aug. 8
cards.teaser: Vero Beach Museum of Art, 3001 Riverside Park Drive, offers free admission on Saturday, Aug. 8, with family activities, gallery sketching, and a lecture on Frank Lloyd Wright's influence on Florida architecture.
cards.body:
Vero Beach Museum of Art will offer free admission on Saturday, Aug. 8. The museum is located at 3001 Riverside Park Drive in Vero Beach. Visitors can participate in Museum in the Studios for families and Sketching in the Gallery from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.

 The museum will also host a lecture titled Frank Lloyd Wright and His Influence on Florida Architecture with Wayne Wood at 3 p.m. Coastal Connections will offer Friendship Bracelet Making during the event. Museum Studios for families and Sketching in the Gallery will also be available during regular hours on Second Saturday.

 The free admission is part of the museum's monthly Second Saturday programming. The museum is located at 3001 Riverside Park Drive in Vero Beach.
